Signature: def broken_links(page: str, parsed: dict, exists) -> list[dict]:

Description: Identifies all relative hyperlinks and image references in a page's prose whose targets cannot be resolved to an existing file in the generated site. Targets are resolved via resolve_link, and their presence is checked using the caller-supplied exists predicate.

Parameters:

  • page (str): The site-relative path of the current documentation page.
  • parsed (dict): The parsed page dictionary produced by parse_page.
  • exists (Callable[[str], bool]): A predicate function returning True if a site-relative path exists.

Returns:

  • list[dict]: A list of problem records, each containing "line" (int) and "target" (str).

Example:

problems = []
for number, target in _links(parsed["prose"]):
    resolved = resolve_link(page, target)
    if resolved is not None and not exists(resolved):
        problems.append({"line": number, "target": target})
return problems

This function calls _links across all prose lines to collect link targets while omitting code spans and HTML comments. Each target is resolved against the current page path via resolve_link. If the target resolves to a site-relative path and exists(resolved) returns False, a diagnostic entry is appended with the target text and line number.

docs.title: mermaid_problems()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def mermaid_problems(source: str) -> list[dict]:

Description: Evaluates the syntax of a Mermaid diagram block to detect conditions that cause client-side rendering crashes. It validates frontmatter headers, checks diagram type declarations against supported Mermaid diagram types, and applies conservative syntax rules to flowcharts and graph diagrams to catch invalid arrow operators, unescaped brackets in labels, and unbalanced delimiters.

Parameters:

  • source (str): The raw text content of the Mermaid diagram block.

Returns:

  • list[dict]: A list of dictionaries with "line" (int, 1-based offset within the block) and "problem" (str), where problem is one of "type", "arrow", "quotes", "brackets", or "label".

docs.title: Phase 1: Header and Diagram Type Validation
docs.text:
lines = source.split("\n")
body = [(number, line) for number, line in enumerate(lines, start=1) if line.strip() and not line.strip().startswith("%%")]
if body and body[0][1].strip() == "---":  # frontmatter (title / config) before the diagram type
    closing = next((i for i, (_n, line) in enumerate(body[1:], start=1) if line.strip() == "---"), None)
    body = body[closing + 1 :] if closing is not None else []
if not body:
    return []
first = body[0][1].strip().split()[0].rstrip(":")
if first not in _MERMAID_TYPES:
    return [{"line": body[0][0], "problem": "type"}]
if not first.startswith(("flowchart", "graph")):
    return []

The function filters out empty lines and comments (%%), then checks for YAML-style frontmatter demarcated by triple dashes (---). The first active line after frontmatter is inspected to verify that its leading token belongs to _MERMAID_TYPES. If the type is unrecognized, a "type" error is reported immediately; if the diagram type is valid but not a flowchart or graph, detailed syntax scanning is skipped.

docs.title: Phase 2: Flowchart and Graph Syntax Scanning
docs.text:
markdown_strings = '"`' in source  # "`multi-line markdown labels`" span lines: quote and bracket counts do not apply
problems = []
for number, line in body[1:]:
    if line.count('"') % 2 and not markdown_strings:
        problems.append({"line": number, "problem": "quotes"})
        continue
    code = re.sub(r'"[^"]*"', '""', line)
    code = re.sub(r"\|[^|]*\|", "||", code)  # edge labels: A -->|label| B
    code = re.sub(r"\w>[^\]]*\]", "x", code)  # the asymmetric shape: id>label]
    unlabelled = re.sub(r"\[[^\]]*\]|\([^)]*\)|\{[^}]*\}", "", code)  # `>>` inside a label is text
    if re.search(r"(?<![-=.])>>", unlabelled):
        problems.append({"line": number, "problem": "arrow"})
    elif re.search(r"\w\[(?![(\[/\\])[^\]\"]*[(\[{]", code):  # A[run(x)] — not the shapes A[(db)], A[[sub]], A[/p/]
        problems.append({"line": number, "problem": "label"})
    elif not markdown_strings and any(code.count(o) != code.count(c) for o, c in ("[]", "()", "{}")):
        problems.append({"line": number, "problem": "brackets"})
return problems

For flowchart diagrams, lines are evaluated sequentially unless Markdown strings (indicated by " + `) are present. The scanner identifies odd quotation mark counts as "quotes", sanitizes label text and edge labels using regular expressions, and checks for unsupported code operators such as raw >> arrows. It also detects nested parentheses or brackets inside standard square brackets that violate Mermaid label syntax unless enclosed in quotation marks.

docs.title: diagram_problems()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def diagram_problems(parsed: dict) -> list[dict]:

Description: Identifies syntax problems across all Mermaid code blocks in a parsed page. It maps the relative block-level error offsets returned by mermaid_problems to absolute line numbers in the documentation file.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): The parsed page dictionary produced by parse_page.

Returns:

  • list[dict]: A list of problem records with "diagram" (int, 1-based index of the diagram), "line" (int, 1-based page line number), and "problem" (str).

Example:

diagrams = [block for block in parsed["blocks"] if block["lang"] == "mermaid"]
return [
    {"diagram": number, "line": block["start"] + problem["line"], "problem": problem["problem"]}
    for number, block in enumerate(diagrams, start=1)
    for problem in mermaid_problems(block["text"])
]

This function filters parsed["blocks"] for blocks whose language tag is "mermaid". For each diagram block, it runs mermaid_problems(block["text"]) and offsets the reported line number by block["start"], producing page-accurate diagnostics.

docs.title: markup_verdicts()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def markup_verdicts(markdown: str, parsed: dict, render) -> tuple[list[tuple[str, tuple, bool | None]], int]:

Description: Compares the CommonMark reading of a document against the output of the site's renderer. It injects tracking markers into intended block elements, renders the document to HTML, and determines whether each element rendered in its intended structural context. This function provides strict verification for markup repair routines such as utils.mkdocs.repair_markup.

Parameters:

  • markdown (str): The raw Markdown text of the page.
  • parsed (dict): The parsed page dictionary produced by parse_page.
  • render (Callable[[str], str]): A rendering function mapping Markdown text to HTML.

Returns:

  • tuple[list[tuple[str, tuple, bool | None]], int]: A tuple consisting of:
    • List of verdicts as (kind, reading, ok), where kind is the element type, reading is a normalized tuple of expected properties, and ok is True, False, or None (if the marker was swallowed by raw HTML).
    • int: Total number of rendered code blocks.

Example:

_lines, marks, found, code_blocks = _rendered_marks(markdown, parsed, render)
verdicts = []
for number, (_index, kind, expect) in enumerate(marks):
    reading = tuple(sorted((key, value) for key, value in expect.items() if key not in ("opener", "cut")))
    where = found.get(number)
    verdicts.append((kind, reading, None if where is None else _mark_ok(kind, expect, where)))
return verdicts, code_blocks

The function calls _rendered_marks to generate intended element markers and collect their rendered HTML positions from _MarkContexts. Each mark expectation is converted into an order-independent tuple of properties, omitting line-specific keys (opener, cut). The mark's rendered context is evaluated using _mark_ok, yielding an exact verdict for every structural element.

docs.title: markup_problems()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def markup_problems(markdown: str, parsed: dict, render) -> dict:

Description: Identifies structural Markdown defects where the site renderer parses content differently than intended under CommonMark rules. It evaluates list items rendered as plain text, flattened nested lists, merged adjacent lists of different types, split lists caused by indented content, tables parsed as raw text, and unclosed or swallowed code blocks.

Parameters:

  • markdown (str): The raw Markdown text of the page.
  • parsed (dict): The parsed page structure from parse_page.
  • render (Callable[[str], str]): The Markdown-to-HTML rendering function.

Returns:

  • dict: A dictionary mapping each markup error category from _MARKUP_KINDS to a list of finding records:
    • "lists_as_text": [{"line": int, "items": int}]
    • "lists_flattened": [{"line": int, "items": int}]
    • "lists_merged": [{"line": int, "items": int}]
    • "lists_split": [{"line": int}]
    • "tables_as_text": [{"line": int}]
    • "code_blocks_not_rendered": [{"line": int, "opener": str}]

docs.title: Phase 1: Mark Placement and Code Block Ownership Mapping
docs.text:
lines, marks, found, _code_blocks = _rendered_marks(markdown, parsed, render)
owners = {}  # rendered code block -> [(mark, opener)] of the fenced blocks whose first code line it shows
for number, (_index, kind, expect) in enumerate(marks):
    if kind == "code" and found.get(number) and found[number]["code"]:
        owners.setdefault(found[number]["code"], []).append((number, expect["opener"]))
problems = {kind: [] for kind in _MARKUP_KINDS}
blamed = set()  # fenced blocks already reported

def blame(opener: int) -> None:
    if opener not in blamed:
        blamed.add(opener)
        problems["code_blocks_not_rendered"].append({"line": opener, "opener": lines[opener - 1].strip()[:80]})

_rendered_marks places invisible Unicode markers at every structural construct and executes the site renderer. The resulting found contexts are inspected to establish code block ownership: for each "code" mark that landed inside a rendered code element (<pre> or Mermaid div), the mark and its opening line are indexed by rendered block ID. The blame helper records code fence failures and prevents redundant reporting of cascaded unclosed blocks.

docs.title: Phase 2: Structural Verification and Element Classification
docs.text:
split_since_item, run, item_listed, last_block = False, None, True, None  # run: list items being folded
for number, (index, kind, expect) in enumerate(marks):
    where = found.get(number)
    if where is None:  # the mark vanished (raw HTML, a comment): nothing to compare
        continue
    if kind != "code" and where["code"]:
        opened = [opener for mark, opener in owners.get(where["code"], []) if mark < number]
        if opened:
            blame(opened[-1])
        run = None
        continue
    problem = None
    if kind == "after":
        continue
    if kind == "item":
        if not where["li"] or where["marker"]:
            problem = "lists_as_text"
        elif where["depth"] < expect["depth"]:
            problem = "lists_flattened"
        elif where["list"] != ("ol" if expect["numbered"] else "ul"):
            problem = "lists_merged"
        elif ("start" in expect or expect.get("continues")) and where["number"] == 1 and not split_since_item:
            problem = "lists_split"
        split_since_item, item_listed = False, where["li"] and not where["marker"]
    elif kind == "content":  # outside the list, or in a shallower item than its own
        problem = "lists_split" if item_listed and (not where["li"] or where["depth"] < expect["depth"]) else None
    elif kind == "table":
        if not where["th"]:
            problem = "tables_as_text"
        elif expect["item"] and item_listed and (not where["li"] or where["depth"] < expect["depth"]):
            problem = "lists_split"
    else:
        knock_on, last_block = last_block in blamed, expect["opener"]
        if not where["code"]:
            if not knock_on:  # else its opening fence was taken as the closer of the block before, reported
                blame(expect["opener"])
            run = None
            continue
        if expect["item"] and item_listed and (not where["li"] or where["depth"] < expect["depth"]):
            problem = "lists_split"

The loop iterates through every placed marker. If a non-code construct was swallowed into a rendered code block (where["code"]), the preceding fence opener is blamed for leaving its block unclosed. List items (kind == "item") are checked to confirm they generated an <li> tag without visible marker characters, achieved the expected nesting depth, matched the ordered/unordered list type, and maintained numbering continuity. Tables and item continuation paragraphs ("content") are checked to verify they were not broken out into sibling blocks or rendered as plain text.

docs.title: Phase 3: Consecutive Error Aggregation
docs.text:
if problem is None:
        run = None
        continue
    if problem == "lists_split" and kind != "item":
        split_since_item = True
    if problem in _LIST_RUNS and run and run[0] == problem:
        between = [line.strip() for line in lines[run[2] + 1 : index]]
        if all(between) or not any(between):  # the same list, tight or loose
            run[1]["items"] += 1
            run = (problem, run[1], index)
            continue
    finding = {"line": expect["opener"] if kind == "code" else index + 1}
    if problem in _LIST_RUNS:
        finding["items"] = 1
        run = (problem, finding, index)
    else:
        run = None
    problems[problem].append(finding)
return problems

For recurring list errors (lists_as_text, lists_flattened, lists_merged), adjacent items belonging to the same list run are collapsed into a single diagnostic finding. The items count on the initial finding is incremented rather than emitting individual findings for every line in the list. Non-list problems or discontinuous list items trigger new finding records in the output dictionary.

docs.title: missing_symbols()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def missing_symbols(parsed: dict, symbols: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:

Description: Cross-references verified symbols extracted from the source code against the text of the documentation page. Any symbol whose terminal identifier never appears in the prose or non-Mermaid code blocks of the page is reported as missing.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): The parsed page dictionary from parse_page.
  • symbols (list[dict]): A list of verified symbol records from facts.py.

Returns:

  • list[dict]: A list of missing symbol dictionaries containing "name", "kind", "parent", and "line".

Example:

text = _page_text(parsed)
words = set(re.findall(r"\w+", text)) | {word.lstrip("$") for word in re.findall(r"\$\w+", text)}
words |= set(re.findall(r"[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*", text))  # an identifier glued to CJK prose: 调用run_flow函数
missing = []
for symbol in symbols:
    name = str(symbol.get("name", "")).split(".")[-1].lstrip("$")
    if name and not (name in words or _names_in(text, name)):
        missing.append({k: symbol.get(k) for k in ("name", "kind", "parent", "line")})
return missing

The function extracts all non-diagram text using _page_text and extracts word sets using regex patterns that account for standard identifiers, PHP-style leading $, and Latin identifiers embedded within CJK prose. For each verified symbol, the terminal name component is evaluated against the extracted words and tested via utils.facts._names_in. Unmatched symbols are returned in the result list.

docs.title: signature_issues()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def signature_issues(parsed: dict, source: str, symbols: list[dict]) -> tuple[list[dict], list[dict]]:

Description: Compares declared code signatures documented in a chapter against verified symbols and the raw source code. Signatures that appear verbatim in the source are accepted immediately. Otherwise, documented parameter lists are compared against verified AST signatures: signatures that only append non-source annotations (such as synthetic type hints) are flagged as embellished, while signatures that add, omit, rename, or reorder parameters are flagged as mismatches.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): The parsed page dictionary from parse_page.
  • source (str): The raw text content of the underlying source code file.
  • symbols (list[dict]): Verified symbol definitions extracted from the source file.

Returns:

  • tuple[list[dict], list[dict]]: A tuple of two lists: (mismatches, embellished).
    • mismatches: [{"line": int, "signature": str, "source": str}]
    • embellished: [{"line": int, "signature": str}]

Example:

flat_source = _collapse(source)
by_name = {}
for symbol in symbols:
    by_name.setdefault(str(symbol.get("name", "")).split(".")[-1], []).append(_head(str(symbol.get("signature", ""))))
mismatches, embellished = [], []
for number, text in _signatures(parsed):
    if _collapse(text).rstrip(":{; ") in flat_source:
        continue
    name = _declared_name(text)
    candidates = by_name.get(name[0]) if name else None
    if not candidates:
        continue
    verdicts = [_compare(_head(text), candidate) for candidate in candidates]
    if "same" in verdicts:
        continue
    if "embellished" in verdicts:
        embellished.append({"line": number, "signature": text})
    else:
        mismatches.append({"line": number, "signature": text, "source": _collapse(candidates[0])[:200]})
return mismatches, embellished

The function indexes verified symbol signatures by terminal identifier name and normalizes the source code using _collapse. For each signature extracted via _signatures, if its collapsed text is not present verbatim in flat_source, it is compared against candidate signatures for that symbol using _compare. Depending on the comparison verdict, the signature is accepted, marked as embellished, or marked as a mismatch.

docs.title: unknown_type_names()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def unknown_type_names(parsed: dict, known_words: set) -> list[dict]:

Description: Detects invented type names inside code spans in Markdown headings (e.g., ###FactClaim``). Any PascalCase identifier appearing in an inline code span inside a heading that does not exist anywhere across the crawled codebase is reported as an unknown type.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): The parsed page structure from parse_page.
  • known_words (set): A set of all identifier tokens found across all crawled repository files.

Returns:

  • list[dict]: A list of problem records with "line" (int) and "name" (str).

Example:

if not known_words:
    return []
found = []
for number, _level, text in parsed["headings"]:
    spans = " ".join(match.group(2) for match in _CODE_SPAN_RE.finditer(text))
    names = sorted(set(re.findall(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*", spans)))  # ASCII: a name glued to CJK text still counts
    found.extend({"line": number, "name": word} for word in names if _TYPE_NAME_RE.match(word) and word not in known_words)
return found

The function extracts inline code spans from heading text using _CODE_SPAN_RE. Word tokens are matched against _TYPE_NAME_RE, which selects CamelCase or PascalCase type names containing both uppercase and lowercase characters. Any token matching this pattern that is absent from known_words is recorded as an invented type name.

docs.title: see_also_issues()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def see_also_issues(page: str, parsed: dict, module: str, module_by_page: dict, facts: dict) -> tuple[list, list]:

Description: Validates the cross-references in the "See Also" section of an API reference page. It compares linked documentation targets against the module's verified dependency graph (depends_on and used_by), identifying links to unrelated modules as well as missing links to known upstream dependencies.

Parameters:

  • page (str): The site-relative path of the documentation page.
  • parsed (dict): The parsed page dictionary from parse_page.
  • module (str): The original module path corresponding to this page.
  • module_by_page (dict): Mapping of site-relative page paths to module paths.
  • facts (dict): The verified facts record for this module from facts.py.

Returns:

  • tuple[list, list]: A tuple of two lists: (unrelated, missing).
    • unrelated: [{"line": int, "module": str}]
    • missing: [{"module": str}]

Example:

depends = {edge["module"] for edge in facts.get("depends_on", [])} & set(module_by_page.values())  # only documented ones can be linked
related = depends | set(facts.get("used_by", []))
linked = {}
pages = set(module_by_page)
section = _see_also_section(parsed, pages, page)
for number, target in _links(section):
    resolved = resolve_link(page, target)
    target_module = module_by_page.get(resolved) if resolved else None
    if target_module and target_module != module:
        linked.setdefault(target_module, number)
unrelated = [{"line": number, "module": target} for target, number in sorted(linked.items(), key=lambda item: item[1]) if target not in related]
missing = [{"module": target} for target in sorted(depends - set(linked))]
return unrelated, missing

The function filters verified dependencies down to modules that have generated pages (module_by_page.values()). It extracts all links from the "See Also" section using _see_also_section and resolves each target to a module. Modules linked in the section that do not appear in depends_on or used_by are reported as unrelated, while required dependencies that were not linked are reported as missing.

docs.title: check_chapter()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def check_chapter( page: str, markdown: str, exists, module: str = "", facts: dict | None = None, source: str = "", known_words=None, module_by_page=None, render=None, ) -> dict:

Description: Executes all checks against a single written chapter and compiles the results into a unified report dictionary. It runs link verification, diagram syntax checks, and unclosed code fence checks on all pages. When a rendering function is supplied, markup fidelity checks are executed. When verified facts are available, it also executes symbol, signature, type name, and dependency checks.

Parameters:

  • page (str): The site-relative filename of the page.
  • markdown (str): The raw Markdown text of the chapter.
  • exists (Callable[[str], bool]): Predicate testing whether a site path exists.
  • module (str, optional): The original source module path. Defaults to "".
  • facts (dict | None, optional): Verified facts record from facts.py. Defaults to None.
  • source (str, optional): The raw source code of the module. Defaults to "".
  • known_words (set | None, optional): Set of repository-wide identifier tokens. Defaults to None.
  • module_by_page (dict | None, optional): Mapping of page paths to module paths. Defaults to None.
  • render (Callable[[str], str] | None, optional): Markdown rendering function. Defaults to None.

Returns:

  • dict: Complete diagnostic report for the page containing all issue categories.

Example:

parsed = parse_page(markdown)
report = {
    "page": page,
    "module": module,
    "broken_links": broken_links(page, parsed, exists),
    "diagram_problems": diagram_problems(parsed),
    "unclosed_fences": [{"line": line} for line in parsed["unclosed"]],
}
if render:
    report |= markup_problems(markdown, parsed, render)
if facts and facts.get("claims") is not None:
    symbols = facts.get("symbols", [])
    mismatches, embellished = signature_issues(parsed, source, symbols)
    unrelated, missing = see_also_issues(page, parsed, module, module_by_page or {}, facts)
    report |= {
        "missing_symbols": missing_symbols(parsed, symbols),
        "signature_mismatches": mismatches,
        "signatures_embellished": embellished,
        "unknown_type_names": unknown_type_names(parsed, known_words or set()),
        "see_also_unrelated": unrelated,
        "see_also_missing_dependencies": missing,
    }
return report

The function first parses the document into structured components via parse_page. Base checks populate broken_links, diagram_problems, and unclosed_fences. If render is supplied, markup_problems is executed and merged into the report. If facts contains valid claims, symbol coverage, signature fidelity, unknown type names, and See Also consistency are evaluated and added to the report.

docs.title: run_chapter_check()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def run_chapter_check(output_path: str, site_dir: str, chapter_files: list, prep_res: dict, standalone: bool = False, render=None) -> dict:

Description: Coordinates chapter verification across all generated files in the documentation suite. It writes the consolidated diagnostic summary to chapter_check.json in output_path, logs structured warnings via utils.output.emit, and returns the final report dictionary.

Parameters:

  • output_path (str): Base output directory where chapter_check.json is written.
  • site_dir (str): Root directory containing the generated documentation files.
  • chapter_files (list[dict]): List of generated chapter file dicts (filename, content, original_path).
  • prep_res (dict): Pipeline preparation results containing module_facts, sources, and known_words.
  • standalone (bool, optional): Whether output is standalone Markdown rather than MkDocs. Defaults to False.
  • render (Callable[[str], str] | None, optional): Markdown renderer for MkDocs pipelines. Defaults to None.

Returns:

  • dict: Aggregated diagnostics summary dictionary with pages, totals, and reports.

docs.title: Phase 1: Context Resolution and Existence Checker Setup
docs.text:
module_facts = prep_res.get("module_facts") or {}
sources = prep_res.get("sources") or {}
known_words = prep_res.get("known_words") or set()
pages = {cf["filename"] for cf in chapter_files}
module_by_page = {cf["filename"]: cf.get("original_path") for cf in chapter_files if cf.get("original_path")}
generated = {"index.md", "full_content.md", "facts.json"}

def exists(path):
    if path in pages or path in generated:
        return True
    if standalone and path.endswith(".md"):
        return False
    return os.path.exists(os.path.join(site_dir, *path.split("/")))

The function extracts facts, source content, and known identifiers from prep_res and builds lookup maps for chapter files. An exists callback is defined to resolve relative file targets against in-memory chapter names, standard generated files, and the filesystem under site_dir. In standalone mode, references to non-current .md files are rejected to avoid linking to stale files from earlier runs.

docs.title: Phase 2: Page Iteration and Event Emission
docs.text:
reports = []
for cf in chapter_files:
    module = cf.get("original_path") or ""
    report = check_chapter(
        cf["filename"], cf["content"], exists, module, module_facts.get(module), sources.get(module, ""), known_words, module_by_page, render
    )
    reports.append(report)
    for problem in report["broken_links"]:
        emit("CHAPTER_CHECK_BROKEN_LINK", page=cf["filename"], line=problem["line"], target=problem["target"])
    grouped = {}
    for problem in report["diagram_problems"]:
        grouped.setdefault((problem["diagram"], problem["problem"]), []).append(str(problem["line"]))
    for (diagram, problem), lines in grouped.items():  # one warning per diagram and kind, its lines listed
        emit(_DIAGRAM_KEYS[problem], page=cf["filename"], line=", ".join(lines), diagram=diagram)
    for kind in _MARKUP_KINDS:  # one warning per page and kind, its lines listed
        if report.get(kind):
            emit(_MARKUP_KEYS[kind], page=cf["filename"], count=len(report[kind]), lines=_line_list(report[kind]))
    for kind in _FACT_KINDS:
        for item in report.get(kind, []):
            emit("CHAPTER_CHECK_DETAIL", page=cf["filename"], kind=kind, detail=json.dumps(item, ensure_ascii=False))

Each chapter file is processed through check_chapter. Diagnostic events are emitted via emit for broken links, diagram failures (grouped by diagram index and error type), and markup issues across all recognized categories. Verified fact mismatches are emitted individually as serialized JSON strings for downstream debugging.

docs.title: Phase 3: Aggregation, Serialization, and Summary Telemetry
docs.text:
totals = {kind: sum(len(report.get(kind, [])) for report in reports) for kind in _COUNTED}
totals["diagrams_failing"] = sum(len({problem["diagram"] for problem in report["diagram_problems"]}) for report in reports)
document = {"pages": len(reports), "totals": totals, "reports": reports}
report_path = os.path.join(output_path, REPORT_FILENAME)
with open(report_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(document, f, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)
emit(
    "CHAPTER_CHECK_DONE",
    pages=len(reports),
    path=report_path,
    broken_links=totals["broken_links"],
    diagram_problems=totals["diagrams_failing"],
    unclosed_fences=totals["unclosed_fences"],
)
if render:
    emit("CHAPTER_CHECK_MARKUP", **{kind: totals[kind] for kind in _MARKUP_KINDS})
if any("missing_symbols" in report for report in reports):  # pages with verified facts
    emit("CHAPTER_CHECK_FACTS", **{kind: totals[kind] for kind in _FACT_KINDS})
return document

The function aggregates issue counts across all pages into the totals dictionary and counts distinct failing diagrams. The complete results are serialized to chapter_check.json at output_path. Summary status events (CHAPTER_CHECK_DONE, and conditionally CHAPTER_CHECK_MARKUP and CHAPTER_CHECK_FACTS) are emitted before returning the aggregated document.

docs.title: source_context()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def source_context(files_data: list) -> tuple[dict, set]:

Description: Prepares source code context for run_chapter_check from raw crawled files. It normalizes file paths to POSIX-style forward slashes and collects the set of all alphanumeric word tokens across the codebase for type validation.

Parameters:

  • files_data (list[tuple[str, str]]): List of (filepath, content) tuples for crawled repository files.

Returns:

  • tuple[dict, set]: A tuple of (sources, known_words):
    • sources: Dictionary mapping normalized file paths to their source text.
    • known_words: Set of all identifier tokens extracted from the source files.

Example:

sources = {path.replace(os.sep, "/"): content for path, content in files_data}
known_words = {word for content in sources.values() for word in re.findall(r"\w+", content)}
return sources, known_words

This helper converts system-specific directory separators to forward slashes across all file paths in files_data and extracts every \w+ token from each file into a unified set.

docs.title: _links()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _links(prose: list) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:

Description: Extracts Markdown hyperlink, image, and reference targets from a list of prose lines. Code spans are masked with spaces and HTML comments are stripped before matching.

Parameters:

  • prose (list[tuple[int, str]]): List of (line_number, text) tuples.

Returns:

  • list[tuple[int, str]]: Deduplicated list of (line_number, target) tuples.

Example:

found = []
for number, line in prose:
    text = _HTML_COMMENT_RE.sub("", _CODE_SPAN_RE.sub(lambda m: " " * len(m.group(0)), line))
    for pattern in (_LINK_RE, _IMAGE_RE, _HTML_HREF_RE):
        found.extend((number, match.group(1)) for match in pattern.finditer(text))
    reference = _REFERENCE_RE.match(text)
    if reference:
        found.append((number, reference.group(1)))
targets = [(number, target[1:-1] if target.startswith("<") else target) for number, target in found]
return list(dict.fromkeys(targets))

This helper iterates over the prose lines, masking inline code spans with space characters to preserve character offsets while preventing false positives. It evaluates the sanitized line against inline link, image, HTML anchor, and link reference regexes, unwraps angle-bracketed targets, and removes duplicate targets via dict.fromkeys.

docs.title: _cells()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _cells(row: str) -> int:

Description: Counts the number of cells in a Markdown table row by splitting on unescaped pipe characters (|).

Parameters:

  • row (str): Markdown table row line.

Returns:

  • int: Number of table cells.

Example:

row = row.strip().removeprefix("|")
row = row[:-1] if row.endswith("|") and not row.endswith("\\|") else row
return len(re.split(r"(?<!\\)\|", row))

The function strips whitespace and removes leading and trailing pipes (unless the trailing pipe is escaped with a backslash). It then splits the remaining text using a negative lookbehind regex (?<!\\)\| and returns the count of resulting parts.

docs.title: _cell_cut()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _cell_cut(line: str, start: int) -> int:

Description: Finds the insertion offset for a tracking marker within a table header row. The mark is placed before the pipe delimiter ending the first cell so that column counts remain intact.

Parameters:

  • line (str): Table header row line.
  • start (int): Starting character offset (e.g., following blockquote prefixes).

Returns:

  • int: Character index where the marker should be inserted, or -1 if no cell pipe was found.

Example:

body = line[start:]
offset = start + len(body) - len(body.lstrip()) + (1 if body.lstrip().startswith("|") else 0)
match = _CELL_PIPE_RE.search(line, offset)
return match.start() if match else -1

The function calculates the starting offset of the first cell by skipping leading whitespace and an optional opening pipe delimiter. It then searches for the next unescaped pipe using _CELL_PIPE_RE and returns its index.

docs.title: _html_block_end()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _html_block_end(lines: list[str], index: int, content: str, previous: str) -> int | None:

Description: Determines the ending line index of a CommonMark HTML block that begins at index. If the line does not begin an HTML block, it returns None.

Parameters:

  • lines (list[str]): List of all lines in the document.
  • index (int): Current line index being evaluated.
  • content (str): Expanded text content of the current line.
  • previous (str): Type classification of the preceding line ("blank", "text", etc.).

Returns:

  • int | None: Line index immediately following the HTML block, or None.

Example:

for start, end in _HTML_RAW_BLOCKS:
    if start.match(content):
        if end.search(content):
            return index + 1
        return next((line + 1 for line in range(index + 1, len(lines)) if end.search(lines[line])), len(lines))
if _HTML_BLOCK_RE.match(content) or (previous != "text" and _HTML_TAG_LINE_RE.match(content)):
    return next((line for line in range(index + 1, len(lines)) if not lines[line].strip()), len(lines))
return None

The function checks content against raw HTML block patterns (such as <pre>, <script>, or comments). If matched, it searches forward for the corresponding closing delimiter regex. Otherwise, if the line matches _HTML_BLOCK_RE or begins a standalone HTML tag not preceded by text, it scans forward until the next blank line.

docs.title: _intended_marks()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _intended_marks(lines: list[str], blocks: list[dict]) -> list[tuple[int, str, dict]]:

Description: Computes the expected CommonMark interpretations for lines whose rendering will be verified. It tracks list nesting depths, paragraph continuations, table headers, and code block boundaries across the document.

Parameters:

  • lines (list[str]): List of document lines with expanded tabs.
  • blocks (list[dict]): Fenced code block dictionaries from parse_page.

Returns:

  • list[tuple[int, str, dict]]: List of (line_index, kind, expectation) tuples, where kind is "item", "content", "table", "code", or "after".

docs.title: Phase 1: Indentation, Fences, and Structural Rules
docs.text:
fences = {block["start"] - 1: block for block in blocks}
marks, stack = [], []  # stack: (content column, numbered) of the open list items, outermost first
previous, after, depth = "blank", None, 0
index = 0
while index < len(lines):
    quote = _QUOTE_RE.match(lines[index])
    prefix = quote.group(0) if quote else ""
    if prefix.count(">") != depth:  # a quote starts or ends: its content is read on its own
        depth, stack, previous = prefix.count(">"), [], "blank"
    expanded = lines[index][len(prefix) :].expandtabs(4)
    indent = len(expanded) - len(expanded.lstrip(" "))
    if index in fences:
        block = fences[index]
        while stack and indent < stack[-1][0]:
            stack.pop()
        first = next((line for line in range(index + 1, block["end"] - 1) if lines[line].strip()), None)
        if first is not None:
            marks.append((first, "code", {"opener": index + 1, "item": bool(stack), "depth": len(stack) - 1}))
        index, previous, after = block["end"], "other", index + 1
        continue
    if not expanded.strip():
        index, previous = index + 1, "blank"
        continue

The parser iterates line by line, handling blockquote prefixes (>) and managing a stack of open list items. When a code fence opener is encountered, open list items with deeper indentation are popped, a "code" expectation mark is added for the first non-empty code line, and the line index advances to the end of the block.

docs.title: Phase 2: Table and HTML Block Detection
docs.text:
base = stack[-1][0] if stack and indent >= stack[-1][0] else 0  # the open item's content column
    following = _QUOTE_RE.sub("", lines[index + 1]).expandtabs(4) if index + 1 < len(lines) else ""
    head, delimiter = expanded[base:], following[base:] if not following[:base].strip() else following
    table = (
        len(head) - len(head.lstrip()) <= 3
        and "|" in head
        and "|" in delimiter
        and _TABLE_DELIMITER_RE.match(delimiter)
        and _cells(head) == _cells(delimiter)
    )
    rule = indent <= 3 and _THEMATIC_BREAK_RE.match(expanded)  # a mark would make it text: the next line gets it
    html = None if table or rule else _html_block_end(lines, index, expanded, previous)
    if after and not (table or rule or html):  # a table's own mark shows where its header landed
        marks.append((index, "after", {"opener": after}))
    if not rule:
        after = None
    if html is not None:
        while stack and indent < stack[-1][0]:
            stack.pop()
        index, previous = html, "other"
        continue
    if rule or (indent <= 3 and _HEADING_RE.match(expanded.lstrip())):
        stack.clear()
        index, previous = index + 1, "other"
        continue

The loop tests whether the current line and the following line form a Markdown table by checking for pipe characters, matching cell counts, and a valid delimiter row. Thematic breaks and raw HTML blocks are identified; if an HTML block is present, list stacks are unwound and processing skips past the HTML block. Any line following a code block receives an "after" marker to ensure subsequent prose was not swallowed by an unclosed fence.

docs.title: Phase 3: List Items and Continuation Paragraphs
docs.text:
item = _LIST_ITEM_RE.match(expanded)
    if (
        item
        and indent < (stack[-1][0] if stack else 0) + 4
        and not (previous == "text" and not stack and (item.group(3) not in (None, "1") or not expanded[item.end() :].strip()))
    ):
        numbered, popped = item.group(3) is not None, None
        while stack and indent < stack[-1][0]:
            popped = stack.pop()
        spaces = len(item.group(4))
        stack.append((item.end(2) + (spaces if 1 <= spaces <= 4 else 1), numbered))
        if expanded[item.end() :].strip():  # an empty item gets no mark: a lone "-" marked would stop being a setext underline
            expect = {"depth": len(stack) - 1, "numbered": numbered}
            if numbered:
                if popped is None or not popped[1]:  # no numbered sibling before it: a new list
                    if item.group(3) != "1":
                        expect["start"] = int(item.group(3))
                else:
                    expect["continues"] = True
            marks.append((index, "item", expect))
        index, previous = index + 1, "item"
        continue
    if table:
        if previous != "text":
            while stack and indent < stack[-1][0]:
                stack.pop()
        marks.append((index, "table", {"item": bool(stack), "depth": len(stack) - 1, "cut": _cell_cut(lines[index], len(prefix))}))
        index, previous = index + 2, "table"
        continue
    if previous == "table":  # table rows run until a blank line or another block
        index += 1
        continue
    if previous in ("blank", "other"):
        while stack and indent < stack[-1][0]:
            stack.pop()
        if stack and indent < stack[-1][0] + 4:  # 4 columns past the item's text: indented code there too
            marks.append((index, "content", {"depth": len(stack) - 1}))
    index, previous = index + 1, "text"
return marks

List items are parsed using _LIST_ITEM_RE, enforcing standard CommonMark rules regarding paragraph interruption and 4-space indentation limits. When a list item is identified, its content column is recorded on stack, and an "item" expectation dictionary is created capturing its nesting depth, ordered/unordered status, and list sequence continuity. Markdown tables record "table" marks, while continuation paragraphs within open list items receive "content" marks.

docs.title: _MarkContexts
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: class _MarkContexts(HTMLParser):

Description: HTML parser subclass that tracks tag hierarchies and detects the locations of injected tracking markers in rendered HTML. It determines whether each marker landed inside a list item, table header, or code block, and records whether a list marker was incorrectly retained as visible text.

class _MarkContexts(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.stack, self.items, self.found = [], [], {}
        self.code = None  # (stack depth, context, text parts) of the code block being read
        self.blocks = 0  # code blocks seen
        self.text = ""  # rendered text of the current block so far

The parser maintains a tag hierarchy stack (self.stack), tracks item indices for ordered lists (self.items), and maps found numerical marker IDs to their contextual metadata in self.found.

docs.title: _MarkContexts._context()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _context(self, code: int | None = None, marker: bool = False) -> dict:

Description: Constructs a snapshot dictionary of the current HTML structural context at the marker's location.

Parameters:

  • code (int | None, optional): Rendered code block sequence number. Defaults to None.
  • marker (bool, optional): Whether the line still starts with an unparsed list marker. Defaults to False.

Returns:

  • dict: Context dictionary containing "li", "depth", "number", "list", "th", "code", and "marker".

Example:

tags = [tag for tag, _classes in self.stack]
lists = [tag for tag in tags if tag in ("ul", "ol")]
return {
    "li": "li" in tags,
    "depth": len(lists) - 1,
    "number": self.items[-1] if self.items else 0,
    "list": lists[-1] if lists else None,
    "th": "th" in tags,
    "code": code,
    "marker": marker,
}

The method inspects self.stack to determine whether the marker is inside an <li> tag, calculates list nesting depth based on enclosing <ul> and <ol> tags, records the active list item index, and flags table headers and code blocks.

docs.title: _MarkContexts.handle_starttag()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public (method on internal class)

Signature: def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):

Description: Handles opening HTML tags during rendering parsing, updating the tag stack and detecting entry into code blocks.

Parameters:

  • tag (str): Lowercase HTML tag name.
  • attrs (list[tuple[str, str | None]]): Tag attributes list.

Example:

if tag == "br":
    self.text += "\n"
if tag in _VOID_TAGS:
    return
if tag in _BLOCK_TAGS:
    self.text = ""
classes = (dict(attrs).get("class") or "").split()
self.stack.append((tag, classes))
if tag in ("ul", "ol"):
    self.items.append(0)
elif tag == "li" and self.items:
    self.items[-1] += 1
if self.code is None and (tag == "pre" or "mermaid-raw" in classes):
    self.blocks += 1
    self.code = (len(self.stack), self._context(self.blocks), [])

The method appends newline breaks for <br>, resets accumulated block text on _BLOCK_TAGS, and pushes tags onto self.stack. For <ul> and <ol>, it initializes a new item counter, and increments the counter on <li>. When entering a <pre> element or a Mermaid diagram block, it marks the start of a code block context.

docs.title: _MarkContexts.handle_endtag()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public (method on internal class)

Signature: def handle_endtag(self, tag):

Description: Handles closing HTML tags, unwinding the tag stack and recording markers located within code blocks.

Parameters:

  • tag (str): Lowercase HTML tag name.

Example:

depth = next((depth for depth in range(len(self.stack) - 1, -1, -1) if self.stack[depth][0] == tag), None)
if depth is None:
    return
if tag in _BLOCK_TAGS:
    self.text = ""
if self.code and depth < self.code[0]:
    for match in _MARK_RE.finditer("".join(self.code[2])):
        self.found[int(match.group(1))] = self.code[1]
    self.code = None
for closed, _classes in self.stack[depth:]:
    if closed in ("ul", "ol") and self.items:
        self.items.pop()
del self.stack[depth:]

The method searches backward from the top of self.stack for the matching opening tag. If closing a code block, all accumulated text parts are joined and scanned for injected markers via _MARK_RE, recording their locations in self.found. It then pops item counters for closed lists and slices the tag stack down to depth.

docs.title: _MarkContexts.handle_data()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public (method on internal class)

Signature: def handle_data(self, data):

Description: Processes text nodes in the HTML document, recording markers in prose or accumulating text for active code blocks.

Parameters:

  • data (str): Raw text content within the current HTML node.

Example:

if self.code:
    self.code[2].append(data)
    return
for match in _MARK_RE.finditer(data):
    line = (self.text + data[: match.start()]).rsplit("\n", 1)[-1]
    self.found[int(match.group(1))] = self._context(marker=bool(_VISIBLE_MARKER_RE.match(line)))
self.text += data

When inside a code block, character data is appended to self.code[2]. Outside code blocks, _MARK_RE.finditer identifies all marker IDs in the text chunk, evaluates whether the preceding line text still starts with a list marker using _VISIBLE_MARKER_RE, and records the resulting _context in self.found.

docs.title: _rendered_marks()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _rendered_marks(markdown: str, parsed: dict, render) -> tuple[list[str], list, dict, int]:

Description: Injects tracking markers into Markdown text, executes the renderer, and parses the resulting HTML using _MarkContexts.

Parameters:

  • markdown (str): Raw Markdown text.
  • parsed (dict): Parsed page dictionary from parse_page.
  • render (Callable[[str], str]): Function rendering Markdown to HTML.

Returns:

  • tuple[list[str], list, dict, int]: Tuple of (lines, marks, found, blocks).

Example:

lines = markdown.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("", "").replace("", "").split("\n")
marks = _intended_marks(lines, parsed["blocks"])
tagged = list(lines)
for number, (index, kind, expect) in enumerate(marks):
    mark, line = _MARK.format(number), tagged[index]
    cut = expect["cut"] if kind == "table" else _HARD_BREAK_RE.search(line).start()  # before a hard break's spaces / "\"
    tagged[index] = line[:cut] + mark + line[cut:] if cut >= 0 else line + mark
contexts = _MarkContexts()
contexts.feed(render("\n".join(tagged)))
contexts.close()
return lines, marks, contexts.found, contexts.blocks

The function normalizes newlines, strips existing PUA characters to prevent collision, and computes intended marks via _intended_marks. Each marker is inserted into tagged before trailing hard breaks or table header delimiters. The tagged text is passed to render, and the HTML output is fed into _MarkContexts to collect marker locations and code block counts.

docs.title: _mark_ok()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _mark_ok(kind: str, expect: dict, where: dict) -> bool:

Description: Validates whether a rendered marker satisfies its expected CommonMark interpretation.

Parameters:

  • kind (str): Marker kind ("item", "content", "table", "code", or "after").
  • expect (dict): Expected structural attributes.
  • where (dict): Actual structural context dictionary recorded by _MarkContexts.

Returns:

  • bool: True if the marker rendered in compliance with its expectation; otherwise False.

Example:

in_item = where["li"] and where["depth"] == expect.get("depth")
if kind == "item":
    return in_item and not where["marker"] and not where["code"] and where["list"] == ("ol" if expect["numbered"] else "ul")
if kind == "content":
    return in_item and not where["code"]
if kind == "table":
    return where["th"] and (not expect["item"] or in_item)
if kind == "code":
    return bool(where["code"]) and (not expect["item"] or in_item)
return not where["code"]

The function verifies that list items render inside <li> elements at the expected nesting depth without visible markers, that content paragraphs inside list items remain nested at the appropriate level, that table headers produce <th> elements, and that code lines and post-code lines are not swallowed by unclosed blocks.

docs.title: _page_text()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _page_text(parsed: dict) -> str:

Description: Extracts all prose and code block text from a parsed page dictionary, excluding Mermaid diagram blocks.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): Parsed page dictionary from parse_page.

Returns:

  • str: Combined prose and non-diagram code text.

Example:

code = [block["text"] for block in parsed["blocks"] if block["lang"] != "mermaid"]
return "\n".join([line for _n, line in parsed["prose"]] + code)

The function collects text from all code blocks whose language is not "mermaid", appends all prose lines, and joins them into a single string.

docs.title: _is_subsequence()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _is_subsequence(wanted: list[str], have: list[str]) -> bool:

Description: Determines whether all tokens in the wanted list appear in the have list in the same relative order.

Parameters:

  • wanted (list[str]): Required sequence of tokens.
  • have (list[str]): Candidate list of tokens.

Returns:

  • bool: True if wanted is a subsequence of have; otherwise False.

Example:

position = 0
for word in have:
    if position < len(wanted) and word == wanted[position]:
        position += 1
return position == len(wanted)

The function uses a single-pass pointer scan over have, advancing position whenever the current element matches wanted[position]. It returns True if position reaches the length of wanted.

docs.title: _strip_decorators()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _strip_decorators(text: str) -> str:

Description: Strips leading decorators, compiler attributes, and comment lines from a code declaration.

Parameters:

  • text (str): Declaration string.

Returns:

  • str: Clean declaration string without leading decorator lines.

Example:

lines = text.split("\n")
while lines and (not lines[0].strip() or _DECORATOR_LINE_RE.match(lines[0]) or _COMMENT_LINE_RE.match(lines[0])):
    lines = lines[1:]
return "\n".join(lines)

The function splits the text into lines and drops leading lines that are blank, match _DECORATOR_LINE_RE (such as @decorator or #[attr]), or match _COMMENT_LINE_RE (such as // or #).

docs.title: _head()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _head(text: str) -> str:

Description: Extracts the head of a declaration up to the line where the parameter list parenthesis closes, truncating any attached function body.

Parameters:

  • text (str): Declaration string.

Returns:

  • str: The declaration header up to the closing parenthesis.

Example:

text = _strip_decorators(text)
name = _declared_name(text)
start = name[1] if name else text.find("(")
if start < 0:
    return text.split("\n", 1)[0]
depth = 0
for position in range(start, len(text)):
    char = text[position]
    if char in "([":
        depth += 1
    elif char in ")]":
        depth -= 1
        if depth <= 0:
            end = text.find("\n", position)
            return text if end < 0 else text[:end]
return text

The function strips decorators and locates the opening parenthesis following the declared function name. It tracks nesting depth across parentheses and brackets. When depth returns to zero, it finds the end of that line and returns the text up to that boundary.

docs.title: _declared_name()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _declared_name(text: str) -> tuple[str, int] | None:

Description: Extracts the identifier name and the character index of its opening parenthesis from a declaration header. Handles JavaScript arrow functions, Go receiver methods, and generic type parameters.

Parameters:

  • text (str): Declaration text.

Returns:

  • tuple[str, int] | None: (identifier_name, paren_position) or None.

Example:

arrow = _ARROW_RE.match(text)
if arrow:
    return arrow.group(1), text.find("(", arrow.end(1))
receiver = re.match(r"^\s*func\s*\([^)]*\)", text)
found = _NAME_BEFORE_PAREN_RE.search(text, receiver.end() if receiver else 0)
return (found.group(1), found.end() - 1) if found else None

The function first evaluates _ARROW_RE to match arrow functions. For standard declarations, it skips any leading Go receiver func (...) and searches for the identifier immediately preceding the opening parenthesis using _NAME_BEFORE_PAREN_RE.

docs.title: _declaration_shaped()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _declaration_shaped(text: str) -> bool:

Description: Determines whether a snippet of code represents a function, method, or class declaration header rather than an invocation, expression, or control statement.

Parameters:

  • text (str): Code snippet to evaluate.

Returns:

  • bool: True if shaped like a declaration; otherwise False.

Example:

text = _strip_decorators(text).strip()
first = (_words(text) or [""])[0]
name = _declared_name(text)
if not name or first in _NOT_DECLARATION:
    return False
if first in _DECLARATION_START:
    return True
if first in ("constructor", "init") and re.search(r"\(\s*[\w$]+\s*:", text):
    return True  # constructor(size: string), init(name: Int) — typed, unlike a call init(language="x")
before = text[: name[1]].rstrip()
before = before[: len(before) - len(name[0])] if before.endswith(name[0]) else before
if before.endswith((".", "->")) or "=" in before:
    return False
if before.endswith("::") and not _words(before.rstrip(":").rsplit(None, 1)[0] if " " in before.strip() else ""):
    return False  # A::b(…) with no type before it is a call; `void A::b(` is a definition
head = _head(text).rstrip()
return len(_words(before)) >= 1 or head.endswith(("{", ":", ";"))

The function filters out statements starting with non-declaration keywords (if, return, await). It accepts tokens starting with _DECLARATION_START keywords (def, func, class) or typed constructors, rejects member calls (object.method(), ptr->call()), and checks for preceding return types or trailing block openers ({, :, ;).

docs.title: _signatures()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _signatures(parsed: dict) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:

Description: Finds code signatures explicitly identified by documentation labels, extracting declarations from inline code spans after bold labels or from the opening lines of code blocks preceded by bold label lines.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): Parsed page structure from parse_page.

Returns:

  • list[tuple[int, str]]: List of (line_number, signature_text) tuples.

Example:

found = []
prose = dict(parsed["prose"])
for number, line in parsed["prose"]:
    found.extend((number, match.group(2).strip()) for match in _LABELLED_CODE_RE.finditer(line) if _declaration_shaped(match.group(2)))
for block in parsed["blocks"]:
    label = prose.get(block["start"] - 1, "").strip()
    if block["lang"] == "mermaid" or not (_BLOCK_LABEL_RE.match(label) and re.search(r"[:\uff1a]", label)):
        continue
    head = _head(block["text"])
    if _declaration_shaped(head):
        found.append((block["start"] + 1, head.strip()))
return found

The function searches prose lines for inline code spans following bold labels using _LABELLED_CODE_RE. It also inspects code blocks preceded by standalone bold label lines (e.g., **Signature**:), extracting their header via _head and retaining only those matching _declaration_shaped.

docs.title: _params()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _params(head: str) -> tuple[list[list[str]], bool] | None:

Description: Parses a declaration header's parameter list into tokenized parameter segments, tracking whether the parameter list reaches a closing parenthesis.

Parameters:

  • head (str): Declaration header string.

Returns:

  • tuple[list[list[str]], bool] | None: (tokenized_parameters, is_closed) or None if no parameter list is found.

Example:

name = _declared_name(head)
if not name:
    return None
params, current, depth = [], "", 0
text = head[name[1] + 1 :]
for position, char in enumerate(text):
    pair = text[max(0, position - 1) : position + 1]
    if char in "([{" or (char == "<" and pair != "<="):
        depth += 1
    elif char in ")]}" or (char == ">" and pair not in ("->", "=>", ">=")):
        if depth == 0 and char == ")":
            params.append(current)
            return [_PARAM_TOKEN_RE.findall(p) for p in params if p.strip()], True
        depth -= 1
    elif char == "," and depth == 0:
        params.append(current)
        current = ""
        continue
    current += char
params.append(current)
return [_PARAM_TOKEN_RE.findall(p) for p in params if p.strip()], False

The function locates the opening parenthesis using _declared_name and iterates through the parameter list, maintaining bracket nesting depth while ignoring comparison operators. Parameters delimited by commas at depth 0 are split into strings and tokenized with _PARAM_TOKEN_RE. The return value indicates whether the parameter list was properly closed.

docs.title: _compare()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _compare(page_head: str, source_head: str) -> str:

Description: Compares a documented signature header against a verified source code signature header, returning a verdict of "same", "embellished", or "mismatch".

Parameters:

  • page_head (str): Documented declaration header.
  • source_head (str): Verified source code declaration header.

Returns:

  • str: One of "same", "embellished", or "mismatch".

Example:

have, wanted = _PARAM_TOKEN_RE.findall(page_head), _PARAM_TOKEN_RE.findall(source_head)
if have == wanted:
    return "same"
page, source = _params(page_head), _params(source_head)
if page is None or source is None:
    return "embellished" if _is_subsequence(wanted, have) else "mismatch"
(page_params, _page_closed), (source_params, source_closed) = page, source
if not source_closed:  # a cut-short verified signature: its complete parameters are a prefix
    source_params = source_params[:-1]
    if len(page_params) < len(source_params):
        return "mismatch"
    page_params = page_params[: len(source_params)]
elif len(page_params) != len(source_params):
    return "mismatch"
if not all(_is_subsequence(want, got) for want, got in zip(source_params, page_params, strict=True)):
    return "mismatch"
return "embellished" if not source_closed or _is_subsequence(wanted, have) else "mismatch"

If the token streams of both signatures match identically, the function returns "same". Otherwise, parameter lists are parsed via _params. If parameter counts differ or any parameter token list fails the subsequence check (_is_subsequence), it returns "mismatch". If all source parameter tokens are preserved in order, the function returns "embellished".

docs.title: _see_also_section()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _see_also_section(parsed: dict, pages: set, page: str) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:

Description: Locates and extracts the prose lines belonging to the "See Also" section of a documentation page. It identifies the section by searching backward through ## headings for the final section containing links to documented chapters.

Parameters:

  • parsed (dict): Parsed page dictionary from parse_page.
  • pages (set): Set of known documentation chapter file paths.
  • page (str): Current page path.

Returns:

  • list[tuple[int, str]]: List of (line_number, line_text) tuples for the section, excluding USED_BY_MARKER.

Example:

starts = [number for number, level, _text in parsed["headings"] if level == 2]
if not starts:
    return []
sections = [
    [(number, line) for number, line in parsed["prose"] if start < number < end and USED_BY_MARKER not in line]
    for start, end in zip(starts, [*starts[1:], float("inf")], strict=True)
]
for section in reversed(sections):
    if any(resolve_link(page, target) in pages for _number, target in _links(section)):
        return section
return sections[-1]

The function segments prose into sections delimited by level-2 headings (##) while filtering out lines containing USED_BY_MARKER. It scans backward through these sections to find the last one containing links to valid documentation pages; if none contain chapter links, the final section on the page is returned.

docs.title: _line_list()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _line_list(findings: list[dict], limit: int = 10) -> str:

Description: Formats a list of line numbers from finding dictionaries into a comma-separated string, truncating with an ellipsis if the list exceeds limit.

Parameters:

  • findings (list[dict]): List of finding records containing a "line" key.
  • limit (int, optional): Maximum line numbers to include before truncating. Defaults to 10.

Returns:

  • str: Comma-separated string of line numbers.

Example:

lines = [str(finding["line"]) for finding in findings]
return ", ".join(lines[:limit]) + (" …" if len(lines) > limit else "")

The function extracts the string representation of "line" from each finding dict, truncates the list at limit items, and formats the output with a trailing " …" if items were truncated.

docs.title: Parsed Page Structure
docs.text:
Dictionary returned by parse_page containing structured Markdown elements.

Field Type Description prose list[tuple[int, str]] List of (line_number, line_text) tuples representing lines outside code blocks (1-based line numbers). blocks list[dict] List of fenced code block records (lang, start, end, text). headings list[tuple[int, int, str]] List of (line_number, level, heading_text) tuples for Markdown headings. unclosed list[int] 1-based line numbers of opening code fences that were never closed.

docs.title: Code Block Record
docs.text:
Dictionary representing an individual fenced code block inside the blocks list of a parsed page.

Field Type Description lang str Lowercase language identifier following the opening fence (e.g., "python", "mermaid"). start int 1-based line number of the opening fence delimiter. end int 1-based line number of the closing fence delimiter. text str Complete text content contained between the opening and closing fence lines.

docs.title: Chapter Check Report
docs.text:
Dictionary returned by check_chapter containing all diagnostic findings for a single page.

Field Type Description page str Relative destination path of the documentation chapter file. module str Source module path associated with the chapter. broken_links list[dict] Broken hyperlink records (line, target). diagram_problems list[dict] Mermaid syntax problem records (diagram, line, problem). unclosed_fences list[dict] Code fence syntax error records (line). lists_as_text list[dict] Optional markup finding: list items rendered as plain text (line, items). lists_flattened list[dict] Optional markup finding: nested lists rendered at root level (line, items). lists_merged list[dict] Optional markup finding: adjacent lists of different types merged (line, items). lists_split list[dict] Optional markup finding: list split across multiple elements (line). tables_as_text list[dict] Optional markup finding: table rendered as plain text (line). code_blocks_not_rendered list[dict] Optional markup finding: code block failed to render (line, opener). missing_symbols list[dict] Optional fact finding: symbols omitted from page (name, kind, parent, line). signature_mismatches list[dict] Optional fact finding: altered parameters or types (line, signature, source). signatures_embellished list[dict] Optional fact finding: added non-source annotations (line, signature). unknown_type_names list[dict] Optional fact finding: undeclared type names in headings (line, name). see_also_unrelated list[dict] Optional fact finding: links to unrelated modules (line, module). see_also_missing_dependencies list[dict] Optional fact finding: missing links to dependencies (module).

docs.title: Consolidated Report Document
docs.text:
Root dictionary structure written to chapter_check.json by run_chapter_check.

Field Type Description pages int Total number of documentation chapter pages evaluated. totals dict[str, int] Mapping of issue category keys to total occurrence counts across all pages. reports list[dict] Array of individual page diagnostic report dictionaries.

docs.title: Rendered Mark Context
docs.text:
Dictionary constructed by _MarkContexts._context describing the HTML element hierarchy at a marker's location.

Field Type Description li bool True if the marker is enclosed within an <li> element. depth int Zero-based nesting depth of enclosing <ul> and <ol> elements. number int 1-based sequential position of the item within an ordered list (<ol>). list str \| None Tag name of the innermost list element ("ul", "ol", or None). th bool True if the marker is enclosed within a <th> table header cell. code int \| None 1-based sequence number of the enclosing rendered code block, or None. marker bool True if the line starts with an unparsed list marker (e.g., *, -, 1.).

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
chapter_check.py implements a passive reporting strategy: it never raises custom exceptions, modifies source documents, or interrupts pipeline execution. Error handling is structured around the following defensive conventions:

  • Missing Verified Facts Handling: When evaluating factual conformance, check_chapter inspects facts.get("claims"). If claims is None (indicating that fact extraction failed or is unavailable for that file), factual conformance checks are skipped entirely, and only structural CommonMark and Mermaid syntax checks are executed.
  • Cascading Code Fence Blame Prevention: An unclosed code fence will swallow subsequent Markdown text and cause following code fences to be parsed as closers. To prevent reporting every swallowed element, markup_problems maintains a blamed set. Once an opening fence is blamed for an unclosed block, subsequent knock-on effects referencing that block are suppressed.
  • Malformed or Truncated Signatures: When tokenizing parameter lists, _params detects unclosed signatures (e.g., multi-line signatures cut short in facts extraction) by returning a boolean is_closed flag. _compare accounts for unclosed signatures by comparing only the complete parameter prefix.
  • Private Use Area Marker Isolation: To ensure that injected tracking markers (...) do not collide with content in user documents, _rendered_marks explicitly strips existing occurrences of  and  prior to marker insertion.

docs.title: crawl_github_files.py
docs.text: Source: utils/crawl_github_files.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
utils/crawl_github_files.py implements the remote source code ingestion subsystem for the knowledge extraction pipeline. It provides automated facilities for retrieving, filtering, and indexing file trees from GitHub repositories. The module supports two distinct operational modes: cloning via SSH through GitPython for Git URLs ending in .git or starting with git@, and tree traversal via the GitHub REST API (v3) for standard HTTPS URLs. This architecture allows the pipeline to ingest remote repositories without requiring external git installations when operating over HTTPS, while retaining support for SSH key authentication and private network clones when required.

The module incorporates multi-layered content filtering and defensive validation to safeguard downstream Large Language Model (LLM) processing stages. Files and directories are filtered through .gitignore specifications (using pathspec's gitwildmatch implementation) fetched either from the cloned directory or directly from the GitHub API. In addition, user-defined glob patterns (include_patterns and exclude_patterns) are evaluated using fnmatch. Binary files and unsupported encodings are filtered out during file reading, and files exceeding DEFAULT_MAX_FILE_SIZE (1 MB) are skipped to avoid memory exhaustion and token budget overrun.

Execution telemetry is deeply integrated with the pipeline's reporting layer via utils.output. Crawl operations emit event-driven status updates, error notifications, size limit warnings, and aggregated ingestion metrics. When interacting with GitHub REST endpoints, the crawler dynamically detects rate-limiting thresholds (HTTP 403 and 429), interrogates the X-RateLimit-Reset header, and implements an exponential backoff wait state if authenticated, or raises actionable configuration exceptions when unauthenticated.
